questions.topic: What a triptych's wings were for
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose served by the wings of a triptych
questions.stem: An architect's brief for a chapel includes a triptych whose two outer panels are hinged to the centre panel and can be closed over it.

options.text: The wings could be closed to protect the central panel and to show a closed, unfigured exterior.
The wings were separate pictures in their own right, sold separately from the centre.
options.misconception: treats the wings as independent saleable pictures

options.text: The wings are shutters for the light, so the centre could be lit only when open.
options.misconception: believes the wings exist to control light

options.text: The wings were added later as a frame, and the centre panel is the original work.
options.misconception: assumes the wings are a later addition

questions.explanation: Hinged wings could close over the centre to shield it and present a plain outer face, which is why a triptych has two. Independent pictures, light shutters and a later frame do not explain hinged construction.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the case is shut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece

questions.stem: In the architect's brief, an altarpiece is 3.0 m tall and its centre panel reaches a vanishing point 1.2 m above the floor. How far above the vanishing point is the top of the altarpiece?

questions.hint: Subtract the vanishing point height from the total.

questions.topic: What a predella does narratively
questions.learningObjective: State the narrative function of a band of small panels below an altarpiece

stimulus.body: The brief describes a chapel altarpiece with a band of small square panels set along its base, below the main image and within the same frame. Each small panel carries a single moment from a sequence, and the frames between them are carved.

options.text: It repeats the main image in a smaller scale so the figure can be seen clearly.
options.misconception: reads the predella as a scaled copy of the main image

options.text: It carries the story of the main subject in successive moments, read left to right.

options.misconception: mistakes the predella for a donor register

options.text: It shows the workshop's tools and the stages of making the altarpiece.
options.misconception: describes the predella as a record of the workshop

questions.explanation: Successive moments carried in separate small panels set below the main image is the narrative function of a predella. A scaled copy, a donor register and a workshop record would each need different evidence.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The convention behind a sacra conversazione
questions.learningObjective: Explain why figures from different ages are shown in one holy conversation
questions.stem: An architect asks in writing why figures from different times are shown together in one holy conversation.

answer.exemplar: A sacra conversazione gathers the Virgin and Child with saints, patriarchs and prophets from different ages into a single shared space, and it does so under a convention that the figures belong to one company and one moment even though their stories are separated by centuries. The convention lets the artist show the whole doctrine of the church in one image, and the shared space asserts that those separated histories meet in the present of the picture.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the convention deliberately places separated figures together as one company in one space. It should not present the grouping as a historical error or as a family portrait.
questions.hint: Say what the convention lets the artist assert.

options.misconception: suggests the board is a fragment

options.text: The border was added after painting, so the figure was drawn first and fitted around.
options.misconception: reverses the order of border and figure

options.text: The board's size and its border set the format, so the figure was composed to fit that fixed shape.
The figure is large because the painter had no skill in small formats.
options.misconception: blames lack of skill for the large figure

questions.explanation: A board of fixed size with a reserved border leaves a field the composition must answer, so the figure is composed for that shape. A later border, a fragment and a painter's inexperience do not explain the measurements.
questions.hint: The panel dictated the field available.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a vanishing point at eye level does for the viewer

options.text: The scene is drawn as though seen from above, from the gallery of a church.
options.misconception: reads a low vanishing point as a high viewpoint

options.text: The scene is drawn as though seen by a person standing in the space, at that eye level.
The scene is drawn as though seen from below, from the floor of the nave.
options.misconception: reads a low vanishing point as a low viewpoint

options.text: The scene is drawn from a fixed mathematical diagram, not from a viewpoint.
options.misconception: claims the vanishing point comes from a diagram not a viewpoint

questions.explanation: A vanishing point at eye level places the viewer inside the scene at the height of a standing person, which is the convention for a picture in a space the spectator occupies. A high or low viewpoint contradicts that.

questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an altarpiece whose painted room continues the church's own space

stimulus.body: The note describes an altarpiece that stands free of the wall on a stone shelf, whose main panel shows a room with a tiled floor and a window that looks onto a distant landscape. The painted architecture continues the height of the real one behind the frame.

questions.stem: According to the note, what spatial idea does the altarpiece carry?

options.text: That the painted room is a model that can be entered and walked through.
options.misconception: reads the painted room as an actual extension

options.text: That the painting is a window onto a separate world entirely outside the church.
options.misconception: treats the painting as a view of an unrelated world

options.text: That the painted room extends the church's own space, so the scene continues beyond the frame.
That the real church is an imitation of the painting rather than the other way round.
options.misconception: reverses which space is the model

questions.explanation: A painted room aligned with the real architecture asserts a continuity between the two spaces, so the scene continues beyond the frame. An unrelated world, an enterable room and a reversed relationship all miss that alignment.
questions.hint: The painted architecture matches the real one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the height of the vanishing point does
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the height of a vanishing point tells a viewer about a space
questions.stem: A design tutor asks in writing what the height of a vanishing point tells a viewer about a painted space.

answer.exemplar: The height of the vanishing point fixes the eye level of the implied viewer, so a horizon at the height of a standing adult places the spectator inside the room with the figures, while a much higher horizon lifts the viewer above the scene and a lower one puts them below the figures. Because the same architecture is drawn differently for each, the height of the vanishing point is one of the surest ways a painter can tell a viewer how they are meant to stand.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the vanishing point height sets the viewer's eye level and thus their relationship to the scene. It should not treat the height as a decorative choice or a fixed rule of one school.
questions.hint: Say where the implied viewer is standing.

options.misconception: suggests the wings came from elsewhere

options.text: The wings were made to close over the centre, protecting it and giving a plain outer face.

questions.hint: The fittings tell you how the wings were used.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an altarpiece is made to relate to its room
questions.stem: An architect asks in writing how an altarpiece is made to relate to the space it stands in.

answer.exemplar: An altarpiece is set against the architecture of the church and aligned with it, and its painted room is drawn so that the ledge, the frame and the real floor continue the space the viewer stands in. Because the picture is a fixed object in a real room, its scale and its horizon are chosen to suit the height of the eye and the position of the altar, and the frame acts as the edge at which the real space is handed over to the painted one.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains the alignment of painted and real space and the choice of horizon to suit the viewer's position. It should not treat the altarpiece as a picture hung anywhere in a neutral room.
questions.hint: Say what the frame does at the edge of the space.

options.misconception: suggests rotating the fixed panel

options.text: Let the painter work at a standard size and have the panel cropped to fit afterwards.
options.misconception: proposes cropping the work to fit the panel

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a predella does narratively
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a predella occupies the position it does
questions.stem: A design tutor asks in writing why a predella is placed where it is and not elsewhere in the altarpiece.

answer.exemplar: A predella is a band of small narrative panels set along the base of the main panel, within the same frame, and its position is the point of it. Placed low, it lets the eye travel upward from a sequence of ordinary moments to the single great event above, and the frame ties the two into one object, so the story reads as the ground from which the main image rises rather than as a separate picture hung nearby.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the low position and shared frame bind the sequence to the main image. It should not treat the predella as an optional extra or as a companion panel of equal rank.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the physical limits of an icon shape its picture
questions.stem: A tutor asks in writing how the physical limits of an icon shape the picture painted on it.

answer.exemplar: An icon is painted on a panel of fixed size, and the painter must compose for that panel rather than the other way round. The shape of the board, the width of the raised border, the direction of the grain and the place left for a small inscription all tell the painter where the head, the hands and the background can go. A composition that ignores these limits is squeezed or cropped, and the conventions of the form exist because they make the limits part of the design.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the board's size and features govern the composition. It should not treat the icon's format as a by-product of the picture's subject.
questions.hint: Say what the board dictates and what it leaves.

questions.stem: A curator asks in writing what the wings of a triptych were made to do.

answer.exemplar: The wings of a triptych are hinged panels that fold over the central panel, and they were made so that the object could be closed, and in closing the centre was protected from dust, handling and the light of the church, while the outer faces presented a plain or heraldic surface suited to the rest of the furniture. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an iconostasis is
questions.learningObjective: Define an iconostasis and explain the reason for its tiers
questions.stem: An architect is asked in writing what an iconostasis is and why it is built in tiers.

answer.exemplar: An iconostasis is the screen of icons that closes the sanctuary of an eastern church, and the tiers it is built in serve the worship that happens in front of it, with the images of the feast and of the season raised higher for the services above and the ordinary ranks of saints below for daily use. The screen is therefore both a wall and a set of images arranged for use, and it governs how the sanctuary is entered and how it is seen.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the iconostasis as a screen of icons closing the sanctuary and explains the tiers by their use. It should not treat the screen as a purely structural wall.
questions.hint: Say what it closes and what it displays.

options.misconception: reverses which space is the model

options.text: That the painted room is a separate place, entered through the frame as a doorway.
options.misconception: treats the frame as a portal to another place

That the ledge is a real shelf added later to support the panel.

questions.explanation: A painted ledge continued by the real shelf makes the two spaces meet without a break, which is how continuity is asserted. A separate place, a reversed model and a later shelf each deny that continuity.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an altarpiece frame relates to the surrounding architecture
questions.stem: A tutor in painting asks in writing how the frame of an altarpiece relates to the architecture around it.

answer.exemplar: The frame of an altarpiece is treated as a piece of architecture in its own right, with a cornice, a sill and often a pair of columns that repeat the divisions of the wall or the niche it stands in. Drawing its mouldings from the same system as the room means that the picture is set into the building rather than propped against it, and the carved frame takes over the job of a cornice, a doorway or a window that would otherwise separate the painted space from the real one.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the frame works architecturally and continues the building's system, integrating the picture with the space. It should not treat the frame as a plain protective edge.
questions.hint: Say what the frame takes over from the room.

answer.exemplar: A sacra conversazione is a picture in which the Virgin and Child appear in company with saints, patriarchs and prophets who belong to different ages, yet are shown sharing one room, one light and one scale. questions.explanation: A good answer defines the convention and explains its purpose in gathering separated figures into one present moment. It should not present the group as a documented meeting or a portrait.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an iconostasis is
questions.learningObjective: Identify a screen of icons that closes the east end of a church
questions.stem: A brief outlines a screen carrying rows of painted holy figures that closes the east end of a church and can be opened for the services.

options.text: It is a shelf for the icons, made to hold them above the altar.
options.misconception: mistakes the screen for a shelf

options.text: It is a rood screen, which carries a loft above the crossing.
options.misconception: confuses the screen with a rood screen and its loft

options.text: It is a fence for the choir, used to keep the singers in place.
options.misconception: mistakes the screen for a choir fence

options.text: It is an iconostasis, the screen of icons that marks and closes the sanctuary.

questions.explanation: A screen of painted figures that closes the east end and opens for the services is an iconostasis, marking the sanctuary. A rood screen, a choir fence and a shelf do not close and open in that way.
questions.hint: Look at what it carries and what it closes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The constraint that shaped the icon
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the field height implied by a stated proportion
questions.stem: An icon panel is 50 cm high. The painter intends the painted field to occupy 70 per cent of the panel's height. What height in centimetres should the field be?
questions.explanation: Seventy per cent of 50 cm is 0.7 times 50, which is 35 cm. The remaining 15 cm is taken by the border and the inscription at the top and bottom.
questions.hint: Multiply the panel height by 0.7.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The constraint that shaped the icon
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a painter asks for the field size before starting

stimulus.body: The note records that a commission is for an icon on a single limewood board of 26 by 34 cm, that the border is to be carved 2 cm wide, and that the painter has asked to know the exact size of the field so that the figure can be composed to fit it.

questions.stem: According to the note, why does the painter need the field size before beginning?

options.text: Because the board must be enlarged if the field proves too small for the figure.
options.misconception: expects the board to be enlarged for the composition

options.text: Because the composition on an icon is worked out for the shape of the field it will occupy.
Because the border can be widened later to correct a badly placed figure.
options.misconception: suggests the border can correct the composition

options.text: Because the field size determines the price the client must pay for the work.
options.misconception: claims the field size sets the price

questions.explanation: The painter asks for the field because an icon is composed for the shape it will occupy, and a fixed board offers no second chance. An enlarged board, a widened border and a price rule do not explain the request.
questions.hint: The board is already decided.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the height of the vanishing point does
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the horizon height must be decided before the mood
questions.stem: A design tutor asks in writing why the height of the vanishing point matters when a painted interior is designed.

answer.exemplar: In a painted interior the height of the vanishing point is the height at which the viewer is asked to stand, and every other decision follows from it. A horizon at the level of a standing adult lets the figures share the viewer's world and makes the room a place one can imagine occupying, while a raised horizon turns the scene into a plan seen from above and a lowered one makes the viewer look up at a space that looms. The architect cannot therefore choose the geometry first and the mood afterwards.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the horizon sets the viewer's position and the mood follows from it. It should not treat the vanishing point as a free decorative choice made after the mood.
questions.hint: Say whose eye the geometry is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a triptych's wings were for
questions.learningObjective: Use construction features to identify panels made to fold shut
questions.stem: A survey records three oak panels, of which the two outer ones are thinner, carry hinges and iron straps, and show a plain marbled ground on their outer faces, while the centre is deeper and richly painted.

options.text: The outer panels are plain shutters, and the marbling is a workshop mark rather than a finish.
options.misconception: treats the marbling as a workshop mark

options.text: The outer panels are the oldest part, and the centre was added in a later campaign.
options.misconception: suggests the centre was added later

options.text: The outer panels are wings made to fold over the centre, and the object is meant to be seen shut as well as open.
The outer panels are painted copies of the centre, made to be seen from either side.
options.misconception: claims the wings are copies of the centre

questions.explanation: Thinner outer panels, hinges, straps and a marbled outer face are the construction of wings made to shut, so the closed state is designed. A later centre, a workshop mark and copied panels do not explain the fittings.
questions.hint: Ask what the object looked like shut.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial logic of an altarpiece
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an altarpiece is set on a shelf against the wall
questions.stem: An architect asks why an altarpiece is set on a shelf against the wall rather than free in the room.

options.text: Because the shelf carries the weight that the wall cannot support.
options.misconception: claims a structural reason for the shelf

options.text: Because a panel set on a shelf can be moved when the room is redecorated.
options.misconception: gives a practical reason for the shelf

options.text: Because a free-standing panel would not cast the shadow the room expects.
options.misconception: invents a reason about shadow

options.text: Because its painted architecture is built to continue the wall and the space of the room.

questions.explanation: A shelf against the wall lets the painted architecture continue the real one, which is the point of the altarpiece's placement. Movability, shadow and load bearing leave the spatial logic unexplained.
questions.hint: Think about the painted room meeting the real one.
